utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. If there are problems with interpretation, please draw our attention. The Defence teams are all here except for Mr. Bourgon, who has informed the Trial Chamber. Prosecution is Mr. Thayer and Mr. McCloskey and I take it that you have got some preliminary issues to raise, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours. We are ready to go and we have the witnesses lined up for the week but if I could go into private session for just one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Can you start again Mr. Haynes, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Certainly. At the conclusion of the evidence of Peter Boering, the Defence for Pandurevic sought to enter into evidence seven documents. They were documents from the Bosnian army command and they were numbered 7D26, 28, 30, 34, 36, 41 and 44. They are currently marked for identification only but they have now been translated into English and are now entered into e-court in their English form and before I forget, I would ask that they be entered into evidence now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there any objection on the part of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So these six -- six, did you say six or seven?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Seven Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: 34 is missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. 34 is missing. So let's I'll go through them again. The following documents tendered by the Defence for accused Pandurevic and which have until now been marked for identification only because they had not yet been translated into English at the time they were tendered, namely 7D26, 7D28, 7D30, 7D34, 7D36, 7D41, and 7D44 are now being admitted into evidence since they have been duly translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Now, any further preliminary issues? Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just to give you an idea what I had in mind for this witness is, as he comes in (redacted) (redacted)then I will, as you had requested, read a summary of his prior testimony. I had just one question to fill in one small blank that didn't come out in the testimony, and then one new exhibit which is based on the prior exhibit where he marked -- he spoke about, about five different areas on an image. Three of the areas got clearly marked in the Court and make sense when you read the transcript. The first two areas he talked about, the Prosecutor didn't have him mark, and so I now had him mark in my office those two areas so we have a new exhibit that he'll just talk briefly about so that the old record is complete and then we -- that should be it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. Any further preliminaries from the Defence teams? I see none. There are two issues or three, maybe, that we'd like to raise with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There are some issues that we would like to raise with you. Thank you for being patient. Last week, on the 20th to be precise, the Prosecution filed a motion seeking protective measures in relation to one further Prosecution witness, who has been rescheduled for this month. This witness basically, if we stick to our time schedule, is due to testify on the 31st of this month. That is a few days before the time limit you would usually have to file a response expires, I mean the time limit for the filing of responses expires on the 3rd of November. Unless you are prepared to state your position now orally, which would enable us then to proceed with an oral decision, we are fixing a -- we are shortening the deadline for the filing of responses until noon of this coming Friday, noon of this coming Friday which would enable us to decide on the protective measures sought by the Prosecution in relation to this witness. We'll come back to you in one of the breaks in case you wish to state that you prefer to deal with it here and now orally, and not file a response. That's number 1. The other issue we'd like to raise is -- relates to the filing of the 23rd of October, that's two days ago, by the Prosecution in relation to the next witness, not the one we are starting now but the one following, and it's a motion, as you would have already noticed, just filed pursuant to the new Rule 92 ter. Prosecution is seeking to admit into evidence, pursuant to this new sub-rule, the transcript taken in the Krstic case of the videotaped testimony of the next witness in a Rule 61 hearing in the Karadzic and the Mladic cases. Due to the imminence of the expected commencement of the testimony of this particular witness, I would, on behalf of the Trial Chamber, like to know whether you have already taken a position on this motion because obviously it needs to be decided before the witness shows up. So again, in order not to prolong or take much time now, we will come back to you on this in the course of the first break. The third thing we wanted to communicate to you is our decision pursuant to what has been raised by Mr. McCloskey earlier on today in the beginning of the session, of this sitting, namely whether it's the case of dealing -- let's go into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we are in open session. There being no further preliminary business to transact, Madam Usher, could you kindly escort the witness in? Isn't he here a bit too early, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Hope springs eternal. But yes, that is who you thought it was, but we'll see him soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Mr. Groenewegen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal. This is the case against Popovic and others, and you are one of the witnesses summoned by the Prosecution. Before you start giving evidence, our rules require that you enter a solemn declaration which I suppose you are already familiar with because you've testified before this Tribunal already. This is tantamount to an oath that you would take in many jurisdictions to the effect that in the course of your testimony, you undertake to speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. Madam Usher, who is standing next to is handing to you now the text of this solemn undertaking. Please read it out aloud and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I understand that you will be testifying in Dutch, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, I will explain to you very briefly what's going to happen, again very briefly because you're familiar with the procedure. Mr. McCloskey, who is lead counsel for the Prosecution in this case will go first. You're a Prosecution witness. Therefore, his will be an examination-in-chief. Basically it's going to be a very short procedure. I don't even know whether there will be any questions or not by Mr. McCloskey. He will, before you start, explain, give a summary of your previous testimony before this Tribunal and then you will -- I will immediately pass you on to the Defence teams, seven of them in this trial, who will in turn cross-examine you. The previous testimony that you have given in this Tribunal has been admitted as evidence according to our Rules but Mr. McCloskey himself now will explain things to you and also summarise the substance of your previous testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: First, can you just tell us your full name?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Paul Groenewegen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you spell your last name for us?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: G-R-O-E-N-E-W-E-G-E-N.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And then if we could go into private session just for a second?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are back into open session. Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It's not maybe that significant but just to have a clear record I believe that the witness was testifying in Blagojevic case, not in Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You're absolutely right. I'm sorry. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Point taken. Thank you for pointing that out, and Mr. McCloskey obviously agrees with you. Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey might agree but does the witness agree or does he remember which case he testified in? Maybe Mr. McCloskey can clear that up?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, You can maybe clarify this with the witness Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The subject we were talking for -- is back when you last testified in July 2003 in the Srebrenica trial; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I am now going to read what is my summary of the testimony from that last trial and we've gone over that before in my office, haven't we?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if anything I say is not true, please stop me and interrupt me. It's meant to be a summary and -- but still if you recognise anything that's not correct, let us know. Okay. Mr. Groenewegen enlisted in the Dutch army in January 1994 when he was 17 years old. He was sent to Bosnia with the Dutch army and served there from January through July 1995. At the time he was a private assigned to Charlie Company based in Potocari with assignments to OP rotations at OP Mike, and OP November. On 11 July, he was on duty in Potocari when Muslim refugees came into Potocari and he described them as exhausted and full of fear. That day, the base filled up with Muslim refugees and then, after that, the refugees sought shelter in a nearby factories. On 12 July, the Bosnian Serb army entered Potocari. That day, he was assigned to the area near the Muslim population to assist with the Muslim population. He stayed in the area of the Muslim population most of the day. He said he was in a line of Dutch soldiers near the Muslim population. He was shown a video of Potocari and the Dutch soldiers and acknowledged that this was the area he was working in. That was Exhibit P47 from the previous trial. That same day, buses arrived, and I am quoting Mr. Groenewegen: "The first people to go there were those who wanted to get into the buses on their own account. The people who didn't want to get in, kind of withdrew into the background and were forced afterwards to get into the buses." That can be found on page 1025, lines 13 to 16 of the prior transcript. To continue the summary: For the Muslims who were unwilling to get on the buses, initially there was only shouting and people were being called names and if they still didn't want to get in, then violence was used by the Serb soldiers. Men were selected from the crowd of Muslims and gathered in an empty house by Serbian soldiers. When the house was full, the men were taken to buses and driven away. The transportation of the Muslim population continued until the evening and then it stopped. On 13 July, Mr. Groenewegen had the same duties he had the day before, which included helping that everything ran smoothly. He was part of a line of Dutch soldiers standing shoulder to shoulder by the crowd of Muslims. The line of Dutch soldiers was extended into the field beyond the main road to help keep watch over the area and make sure that individual Muslims did not wander off too far. Mr. Groenewegen was in that line farthest from the road. At one point that day, his attention was drawn to shouting and he saw a man from the crowd dressed in civilian clothes on the road, who had been taken by some Serbian soldiers. About ten or 15 minutes after seeing this Mr. Groenewegen's attention was drawn again to this same man. This time he saw the man a short distance away placed up against the wall of a nearby house by Serbian soldiers. Mr. Groenewegen saw a Serb soldier shoot the man from a distance of about three metres. The man collapsed after being shot. Mr. Groenewegen noticed other Serb soldiers look to the area of the shooting after the shot was fired but they just continue their activities. Mr. Groenewegen stated he was about 30 metres from where the man was shot. Mr. Groenewegen stated that in his statement to the OTP on 29 September 1995, he had shifted the dates one day but was certain about the dates he mentioned in his testimony at that last trial. So when he mentioned in his previous statement 11 July, that should have been 12 July. In that statement. Mr. Groenewegen acknowledged that he had not mentioned in any previous statements that the Muslim population who refused to get on the buses were first insulted and then forced on to the buses. And he acknowledged that this testimony during that trial was the first time he had reported this, being the date of his testimony 10 July 2003. Mr. Groenewegen stated that the BiH army was in the enclave and that -- what he meant by that was men with weapons ready to fight. Mr. Groenewegen marked an aerial image which was Exhibit P50 from the former trial. The position of the civilian when he first noticed him was marked with an A on that aerial image. He made an X on the aerial image where he, Groenewegen, was standing when he saw the civilian, and he drew a line to the X which meant to depict where he had originally been and where he had gone to point X. Mr. Groenewegen had marked with a solid dot the area he saw the civilian shot, where the civilian was shot. And Mr. Groenewegen, can you confirm what I said to be an accurate summary of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I did not notice any errors.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's a poorly stated question. Was that -- was what I said accurate to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, I just want to ask one question which didn't actually come out in the testimony. When you first saw that man, the civilian man, in the crowd with Serb soldiers around him, how many Serb soldiers did you see around him in the crowd?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Four.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And when you saw the man shot, how many Serb soldiers were standing around him then?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: There were also four.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, do you remember in my office I showed you an aerial image from the prior trial?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then I brought out a new image and asked to you mark some things on it?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to bring that -- up that image on the screen and ask you to explain briefly what those markings were, and that's 65 ter number 02266.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have a hard copy of it? I'm being told that it's a big document that takes a long time to upload. Anyway, it's uploading or downloading anyway. So we got it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Zero in a little bit on those markings. A little more. [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry. Yeah, if you could zero in on the red markings and centre them a little bit higher? Okay. One more. Actually that's pretty good.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Groenewegen, do you see the -- well, let's -- the new markings you did in my office?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And could you -- well, let's pick one out and tell us what it is. Describe which marking you're referring to. I see one that looks like a pear and one that looks like a circle and then an A, X, and a dot. So which ones are the new markings?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: A is the spot where I saw the man taken out of the crowd.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: The X is the place where I walked to from where I witnessed the execution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: And the closed point is where I -- the solid point is where I saw the man shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What is that line that is connected to the X?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: That's the area where I was walking around that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And what are the other markings on the map? The pear marking in red, for example?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: The red circle marked H is the house to which the men were taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So when you say where the men were taken, what are you referring to, just so it's clear?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: The Muslim men in the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And what about the pear-shaped mark, what is that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: That's the area where I was walking around that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And did you make all these marks in my office on Friday?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And the -- did you look at your old exhibit and confirm that the A and the X and the dot were what you thought they were from the old exhibit?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Yes. They are at the same spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Who is going first? Mr. Zivanovic is lead counsel appearing for accused Popovic in this case and he will be cross-examining you. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Groenewegen, can you please explain what your role was and what was the role of other UN troops during the evacuation of civilians from Potocari which lasted over two days?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: We were asked to assist the population and to take the sick to the appropriate spots.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Together with the other troops, did you make a line separating the Muslim civilians and refugees on the one side from the soldiers of the VRS on the other side?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was the object of that separation to prevent a contact between these two groups, between the civilians on the one side and the VRS soldiers on the other side?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In your testimony in the Blagojevic case, you said, amongst other things, that one of the reasons for doing that was to prevent an aggression on both sides. Do you remember that you said that in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain what you meant when you said that you tried to prevent any aggression on any of the sides? What aggression did you have in mind when you said that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Would you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What aggression did you have in mind, and this is just a follow-up on my previous question, what kind of aggression on any of the sides did you try to prevent by separating the sides?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: We saw that the soldiers were approaching the population aggressively through physical violence and we tried to prevent that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this applies to only one side. However, you mentioned that you feared aggression on both sides. Can you then explain what kind of aggression did you expect on the other side?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Not off the top of my head, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: During that testimony, you also mentioned for the first time that you saw some people who had been forced to get on the buses. Do you remember that? Do you remember that you said that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Correct. I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you now remember whether this applied to women and children only?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Women and children, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did this apply to men as well?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: They were separated elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did this occur once the women and the children had been separated from the men? In other words, was that the main reason why some of the refugees, and I mean women, did not want to leave without the male members of their families?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us whether you and other UN troops, i.e., your officers, did something in that situation, in a situation where a certain number of refugees would not get on the buses without the male members of their families? Was anything done and, if so, what was done?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: When such situations occurred, we intervened by getting in between them, but because of the confusion and the language barrier, we were not able to be effective in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before giving testimony in the Blagojevic case, you provided another testimony, also at this Tribunal, and you have also provided two written statements. Do you remember that? One of them was provided to the investigators of The Hague Tribunal and another one was given during the parliamentary investigation to the Dutch authorities? Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you stated that you were present --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just a moment. I apologise to you, Mr. Zivanovic, but I want to make sure of this. The transcript shows your question as intending to suggest to the witness that apart from testifying in Blagojevic, he has also testified in some other case which I don't think is the case, is it? He gave statements but did not testify apart from in Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I -- I believe that he testified in the Karadzic and Mladic case. This was not a trial. This was the case of transferring the case to The Hague Tribunal, and this is the testimony that I had in mind. I believe that this was in the form of a testimony rather than a statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. All right. Then your question was transcribed well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You stated that you were present when the refugees left Potocari on the 12th and the 13th of July, and I'm sure you remember that.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement provided to the investigators of The Hague Tribunal, you stated that on the 12th of July, you did not see any men having been separated from the women and the children. Do you remember that statement? Can you confirm that you stated that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: That does not sound credible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown his statement, which is on the Prosecutor's list of exhibits, the statement was provided on the 29th July 1995 -- 29th of September 1995, on page 3.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Sorry, what is the 65 ter number of the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid I don't have it. On the list that we have, we cannot find this number. It has not been provided to us, as far as I can see. I only know that it is on page 2. This is the first one on page 2. You will find it on page 3. And the paragraph in question is number 8, paragraph number 8. The paragraph starts with the words, "[In English] [Previous translation continues] ... and to be taken away." [Interpretation] And here you will find the sentence, [Previous translation continues] ... "were not split up on that day."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that I have your statement -- no, I don't have your statement in Dutch. It seems that your statement is only in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can anyone help us? I would imagine that there should be one in Dutch. In fact, Mr. McCloskey has it and I suggest that we do what we did with Colonel Boering, put it on the ELMO so that the witness can see what is recorded in his own language. Or make it easier, I think he's the only one who is interested in seeing it in the Dutch language, no one else. Maybe the interpreters who are translating from Dutch. Yeah, okay. So then put it on the ELMO, please. You have to -- it doesn't show the paragraph, usher. You have to put it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says paragraph 1 in Dutch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But he was being shown the previous page. [Dutch spoken]. Yes. You could perhaps repeat your question, Mr. Zivanovic, and the witness can proceed with answering it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My question is this: Can you see this passage in Dutch and can you see that it reads that on that day, the refugees were not split up, and the day in question is the 12th of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: That's correct. I've seen that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: At that moment, your memory of the events was very fresh and I would assume that what you stated on that day was correct.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I thought so too, but the dates have shifted by one day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is true that the dates have been shifted in this statement. However, we are still talking about day 1 of the evacuation. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain the reason why you changed this statement of yours later, saying that the separations took place that day as well, the separations of men?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: At each statement I tried to describe the situation as close as possible to the truth. If anything I stated is not entirely accurate I would be happy to correct that. As far as not separating the men, I've revised that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, are you trying to tell us that what you said then was not true, what you said in your statement was not true?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would prefer you to choose whether to use the word "true" or "correct" or "not correct" because there is a fundamental difference between something which is not true and something which is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you very much. I will rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you give a correct statement on the 29th of September 1995, that the refugees on the first day of the evacuation were not separated?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: That would not have been accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the statement you provided to the Dutch authorities, you said that on the 12th and 13th of July, a total of 400 men were separated from the women. Do you stand by that statement?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: That has been my estimation and I stand by the estimation. I cannot give any accurate figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that the men who were separated were taken to a house, and you explained that in your previous statements, you explained that you saw them being taken there but you could not see if they were coming out of the house and where. Do you recall these words of yours? You told this to The Hague investigators and to the Dutch authorities.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: That is correct. I have seen no buses with men leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement to the Dutch authorities, you also said that you were present when a truck with bread arrived and the bread was distributed to the refugees. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that this was filmed by Serbian television, a TV crew that came together with the Serbian soldiers. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you also said that when the crew stopped filming this distribution of bread, that they continued to distribute the bread to the refugees.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement, you also said that from the 13th of July, after the evacuation of the refugees, you remained in Potocari until the 20th of July, cleaning up what was left behind. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: That's correct. I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember if a lot of things were left behind after the refugees left, whether there were many things left behind by the refugees close to the, or around, the UN base in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I recall people had very few belongings with them, and that therefore very few goods were left behind in the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you personally clear these things or was this something that other people did?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I didn't busy myself with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Zivanovic. Who is next? Which Defence team is going next? Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Meek is appearing for Colonel Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise. It's six minutes until we normally take our break. I would ask if we could possibly break early.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. Meek. Judge Kwon is right. We break at quarter to 4.00. So you have ample time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Meek. Who is next? Madam Nikolic is appearing for Mr. Nikolic in this case. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Groenewegen. I'm going to put a few questions to you about these events you were a witness to on the 12th and the 13th of July 1995. In your earlier testimony, you spoke about the arrival of the soldiers at Potocari and what was going on there on the 12th and the 13th. We will go back particularly to the 12th of July. You noticed different kinds of uniforms. Can you describe the uniforms for us, please?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: There were camouflage suits in purple tints [as interpreted], in green colour and also some people were dressed in partial camouflage suits with black pants.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: There were also units with dogs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And you assumed that they belonged to the Bosnian Serb army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That's what I assumed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You also noticed camouflage uniforms with different markings, with different insignia, emblems?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: They certainly must have been around but I cannot recall them in my mind, these insignia that is, right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you know to which units those soldiers belonged?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You witnessed a killing which you described.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The people who surrounded the person who was executed were wearing camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: These uniforms didn't have unit insignia?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: No. I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: These soldiers could have belonged to any military or paramilitary unit that happened to be in Potocari at that time?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Given the way they behaved, interacted with the other soldiers, that would be very improbable.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: But you don't know which units the soldiers belonged to?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: The camouflage suits were identical to those used by the vast majority of the soldiers present at the venue, at the site.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: But you don't know which units those soldiers belonged to?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: That is correct. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Nikolic. Who is next. Mr. Stojanovic? Mr. Stojanovic, together with Mr. Lazarevic, are appearing for accused Borovcanin here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Groenewegen. I'm going to go in order, attempting to proceed in the same order that you were responding to questions by Mr. McCloskey. On the 11th of July 1995, you were at observation post Mike; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: On the 11th of July, I was at the compound in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When did you come from the Michael observation post to the Potocari compound?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I can't give the exact dates but it was a few days before the 11th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: After you left the Michael observation posts, were there any members of the Dutch Battalion left at the Michael observation post?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Yes. A full unit of 12 soldiers remained.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please help us? How long did they stay or until when did they stay at the Michael observation post?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I wasn't present there, and I do not know when they left this observation post.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see them at the UN compound at any point on the 12th or the 13th of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Yes. I've seen them in the valley as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What do you understand as the valley? Where is that located?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I mean the surroundings of the Potocari compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that a number of the Dutch Battalion members from the Michael observation post were with the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I haven't learned about that myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the night of the 11th to the 12th of July, so the evening before the evacuation began, where were you?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: We spent the night in the bunker of the Potocari compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please help us and tell us when, on the first day of the evacuation, and I will say that that was on the 12th of July. In your opinion, when did the evacuation actually begin?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: The evacuation started from the moment the buses arrived. At what point in time that happened, I can't say off the top of my head, but this should be present in my written statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you try to give us a time, whether it was in the morning or in the afternoon of that day, please?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: It must have been in the early morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Incidentally, I would like to ask you what was the reason why you came to the Potocari compound before the rest of the members of the Dutch Battalion from the Michael observation post?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: My departure to the compound was part of the normal rotation schedule.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 12th, in the morning, when the evacuation began, who did you receive your personal orders from for activities that you were supposed to do?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: We received orders from Mr. Schaik [as interpreted] . I do not exactly remember his precise rank. It must have been Sergeant Major.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just to clear it up, I'm sure the interpreter didn't catch it but he said "van Schaik."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I did hear him but Mr. Groenewegen, could you confirm that, please? Who did you receive orders from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sergeant Major van Schaik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And what precisely was the order that you received that day from Sergeant Major van Schaik? What did it state exactly?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I cannot remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you try to help us, then, and tell us what you yourself did on that day, the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: We were told that we should offer assistance to the population, that we should survey the state of the wounded and the general population.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I understand your answer. I understood it earlier when you gave it. But actually what exactly did your work entail, this assistance or help to the population, as you said?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I was a part of those who were in between the soldiers of the Serb army and the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And what were you are doing there, Mr. Groenewegen?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: We looked at the situation. For as far as possible we dealt with the skirmishes between the army and the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And what was your role in these skirmishes? What was your activity? What were you doing specifically?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I did not personally intervene. Colleagues around me were involved in them. I was the line between the population and the army, and I walked further south, and later that day I witnessed the execution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I understood that you said that the execution happened on the second day of the evacuation. Am I correct? Now you are saying something different.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: What day are we talking about? The 12th?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You're right. We are talking about the 12th of July 1995.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Then I apologise. I did indeed confuse the execution with that same day, but I witnessed it the day afterward.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 12th, thus you were standing between the refugees and the Bosnian Serb army, and you were assisting the refugees. Were you doing that the whole day of the 12th of July, the first day of the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: We weren't there. Could you please help us and tell us how you saw it? How did the evacuation proceed?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Well, on the one hand, there were an awful lot of people that we tried to help each and every one of them by giving them any information we could, by providing them with water. We tried to assist women with children.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you helping them as they were boarding the buses? Were you trying to prevent this panic from breaking out that you talked about?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what number of people were going towards the buses, and how?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: All I can give you is a rough estimate. It was so disorganised that day. I saw so many people. I estimate that there were thousands, and it was not a smooth process.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that at one point, all the refugees, everybody, wanted to go towards the buses?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Who was it who decided which groups of refugees should go to the buses? Were these from the army of Republika Srpska or members of the Dutch Battalion or did they decide this together?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I know one thing for certain: It was not decided by DutchBat people.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Am I correct if I say that you, together with members of the army of Republika Srpska, were forming human barrier which was separating the refugees from the place where the buses were?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps this is a good point to stop for the break, because after, I will move on to other questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. We'll have a 25-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. There is one minor thing that we would like to draw your attention to in relation to the testimony, to the transcript, rather. Please go back to page 29, line 20. Mr. Stojanovic asked the witness, were you helping them as they were boarding the buses? And then a second question, the same breath, were you trying to prevent this panic from breaking out that you talked about? And the answer is that that's correct, but this is not clear. Maybe that's correct refers to the last question, but we don't have the answer in the transcript to the first question, which I did hear the witness give. So Mr. Groenewegen, you were asked by Mr. Stojanovic, "Were you helping them as they boarded -- they were boarding the buses?" What was your answer to that? Or what is your answer to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not help people board the buses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And when you -- you were asked were you trying to prevent this panic from breaking out that you talked about, and what was your answer, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We did our best to prevent panic among the people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Please Mr. Stojanovic, he's back, I give him back to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Groenewegen, we left it off at the wall that was between the buses and the refugees. This was your answer. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Bearing in mind your answer to the Honourable Chamber's question, can you tell us how the refugees managed to go through that human wall and get on the buses? Who was it who gave them the permission to go through that wall?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's compound and will create a similar problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think if you can break it down, Mr. Stojanovic. Mr. McCloskey is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: My question to you is this: Who was it who let the refugees go through and get to the buses?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: That was imposed upon us by the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that you, members of the DutchBat, were the ones who were in a position to let the refugees, the civilians, go through and get to the buses?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you also make a decision as to the fact which group of refugees would make it to the buses?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I did not take any decisions about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did members of the DutchBat, not you personally, make decisions as to how many refugees they should let through and allow to get to the buses?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, then. Would you please tell us this: On the 12th of July, where did you see the men being separated from the women and the children? At what spot was that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: It happened to the side of the crowd.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that behind the human wall, or rather the selection was being carried out between the human wall and the buses, in that area there?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: No. Behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please be more precise? Behind what? Where was this selection carried out?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I could tell you the most clearly, I've indicated it on the map by the letter A, where I saw the men removed from the crowd. That was where, as far as I could see, the men were being removed from the crowd.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me try and put it this way: Would the refugees, the children, the women, and the men, first go through the human cordon where you were and were they separated only after that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: No. Before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you something else. Do you know a person called van Duijn, who was also a member of the DutchBat?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Yes. I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was he there on the 12th of July, on the first day of the evacuation, together with you?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I don't remember seeing him that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And now try and tell us this: There was a human wall, which separated the refugees from the buses, and you are telling us that before the refugee column went through that human wall, the men got separated from the rest of the column? Is that correct? Is that a correct understanding of your answer?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The men who were separated, did they also go through that human wall before they arrived at the house that you have mentioned, where they would be accommodated?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: No. They were escorted past it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, then. Thank you. And let me put my last question about the 12th of July. On that day, how long did you stay on the spot of the evacuation? How late in the day was it when you left that area?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I did not leave the evacuation site. We spent the night outside there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, then, that during that night, between the 12th and the 13th of July, some refugees were accommodated within the UN base?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: During that night between the 12th to the 13th of July, were there any troops of the VRS in the area where you were, or did they leave that area?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: They had left that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please assist us and tell us this: When did the evacuation of the refugees who were accommodated in the UN base start?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I can't tell you anything about that because I remained outside the base.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Groenewegen, we heard several witnesses here who have told us that during the night between the 12th and the 13th, there were suicides, that a lady giving birth died, that a person hanged himself, that a person committed suicide in the bathroom. Did you also hear about these stories, rumours and comments about such events that allegedly took place during that night?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I only heard them. I did not actually experience them myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, then. Let's move on to the second day of the evacuation, the 13th of July 1995. Could you please tell us when the evacuation started on that second day?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: It must have been early in the morning, I believe from about 7.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: We've heard a witness here who said that the evacuation preceded the arrival of the VRS troops. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: No. I would not have said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What would you say? What happened?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I cannot accept or corroborate statements by other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In your experience, according to your memory, would you say that the evacuation started before VRS members arrived?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: No. As far as I remember, it only started once they were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Which members of the DutchBat were there between the 12th and the 13th of July and in the morning of the 13th of July, or, rather, which was the highest-ranking officer of the DutchBat that was there?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you. I know who addressed me directly. As to whether he was the highest-ranking officer at that point, I couldn't tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you give us the name of the officer who addressed you directly?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: That would have been Captain Koster.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 13th of July, on the second day of the evacuation, did you also see people being separated or not?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The men who had been separated from the rest of the group, where were they taken to?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: They were taken to the same house as the day before.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we now be provided with the sketch or the photography that the Prosecutor used, P20266?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the number of the document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stojanovic, could you kindly repeat the number of the document? I think it's P2266.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, Your Honour. It is P2266, the same document that the Prosecutor used in their examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there a problem or is it going to take the usual time to load?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. In the meantime, if you can move on to some other question?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Groenewegen, are you familiar with the term "White House"?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Am I right in concluding that on the 12th July, the first day of the evacuation, and on the 13th of July, the second day of the evacuation, the men who had been separated from the rest of the group were taken to one and the same house?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Am I also right in saying that in the photo that we will soon see, you put a letter H next to the house that we have been talking about today?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now look at this photo?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The image is available. Do you want the technician to zoom into the marked parts?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please. Only -- thank you very much. This is good.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us repeat, Mr. Groenewegen. Would you agree with me that the house marked by a letter H is the house where the men were taken to on both days, on the 12th and on the 13th of July 1995? Am I right?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that on the 13th of July, the refugees were on the road marked by a letter A in this photo? And in the vicinity of that road as well? Would that mean that the spot marked by the X in this photo was the point of execution among the refugees who were there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey? I think he has explained that already, Mr. Stojanovic. He has explained, A he's explained the line, the X, the dot. Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, as well as the compound nature of that question makes it impossible to answer clearly as well, and of course, it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he's explained X -- I mean I won't repeat it myself although I remember but he did explain what the X is, what the dot is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour. I will rephrase the question because I'm trying to make a different point, an entirely different point, if you will allow me to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The place marked by X, how far is it from the place where the group of refugees could be found?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: All I can do is estimate. I estimate about 70 or 80 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could the refugees see the execution? Was that in their line of vision?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. That calls for a conclusion, speculation, and it's compound as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But at least he can actually state whether, in his opinion, they were in direct -- they had a direct vision or view of -- or whether their view would have been obstructed. So it's not complete speculation. His answer may be based on what he could observe at the time or could have observed at the time. So, Mr. Stojanovic -- do you need to us repeat the question to you, Mr. Groenewegen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The question is whether the crowd was able to perceive the execution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's possible, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could they also hear shots, bearing in mind the 70-metre distance that you've mentioned in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is where speculation comes in.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will rephrase this part of the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you yourself hear the shots?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I definitely heard the shots.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's a misstatement of the evidence. I think we have -- depending on which evidence he's referring to which means it would be vague but the killing he's talking about is a one-shot killing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I think before he did mention that there were shots.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's correct. That's why I say it's as well as vague and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So you need to be precise, Mr. Stojanovic, which shots are you referring the witness to, whether it's that one shot that allegedly killed that man or whether it's other shots that may have preceded or followed?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Groenewegen, did you personally hear that one shot which accompanied the execution?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And I will be finishing with this: Did you inform your superiors about this incident?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Yes, I did that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us when you told them?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I reported it unofficially late that evening, and the next morning I was requested to make an official statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would now like to ask you to look at Exhibit 2D32 on e-court. And before we see the text on e-court, Mr. Groenewegen, I would like to tell you and ask you the following. If I'm not mistaken, this is a report or a statement that you provided on the 23rd of July 1995, at 1200 hours, at the Pleso base where you say in the last sentence, "Groenewegen reported this incident the same evening." Do you see that? Do you agree? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the Blagojevic case, on page 1036, lines 10 to 14, and this is a statement that we used today, in response to a question by the Prosecutor whether at any point you had the opportunity to report what you saw, you replied, "That day I did not." Then there was the question, "When did you report this?" And you replied, "The following morning." My question is: When did you inform your superiors about this incident?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Late that same evening, I told my direct superior, and nothing else was done about it that night. And the next morning, I had to make an official statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Who was the immediate superior to whom you conveyed this on the 13th in the evening?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I don't remember that. There were a lot of people around me, and everybody had his own opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you specifically recall who was the superior officer to whom you conveyed this?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: On what day do you mean? The evening or the next morning when I made my official statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The 13th. I'm speaking of the 13th of July, in the evening.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I'm not certain who was around me so I'm not going to mention any names.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you mention the name of the senior officer to whom you reported the following day, on the 14th?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: That was Lieutenant Schotman.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was Major Franken informed about the incident, if you know?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I consider it highly likely that that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would now like to look at a photograph on the e-court of this area, and this is Exhibit EC 18. It's a Prosecution exhibit. If it's a problem, perhaps if it's not possible to use both at the same time then maybe the usher can place that on the ELMO. Mr. Groenewegen, can you recall --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, stop, stop, because -- usher, can you ask the witness to leave the room for a moment, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, usher, can you turn that photo the other way around, upside -- it is, turn it upside down. Yes. Now, this is why I sent the witness there because this is all marked. There is the "White House" marked, UN, there is the body marked, the bus compound, the UN, and it's also signed by someone. So I wouldn't like the witness to be asked questions and expect answers from him looking at a map which is already, or an image which has already got markings on it and I didn't want to say it in his presence. So I'm sure that there is another image like this that we can make use of. Perhaps with the help of the Prosecution case manager, we can identify it, and then we can upload it or download it from --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's P01516.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Josse. Now you got the message. I don't think it's something you would contest any one of you. Please bring the witness in again but remove that map.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may digress for just a moment, I know that this is marked and all I wanted to do was to clarify an inconsistency that will appear in this marked photograph, marked by Major Franken. The body of -- location of a body that the witness mentioned is other than the way he described it. So I wanted to clarify with him what is actually correct, in view of the fact that he said today that he thought that Major Franken had been informed about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey? If -- I thought I saw you standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. The -- I think the witness will -- I think it's clear from -- if we go back to Major Franken that the area will be different but I think the Court can sort that out. I think there -- it's problematic like you said to put these documents that have been marked with someone else. I mean I think the point will be made clearer once the -- I mean, it's already clear because -- and I can tell you that it will be two different places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but the whole thing was this: First let him see this image and let him mark, put marks on this image. If it's the case of looking at the other one afterwards then we'll see if it's case of looking at the other one but first let him mark the map, put his markings on a clean map or a clean image.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I mean, he -- well, you never know but he should put it the same place that he put it for me because that's the only body he knows about but we can have him do it on cross. You never know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's bring him in again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If we could possibly zoom in a bit, at least once. I think we need to see the upper part too, because this -- yeah, okay. Let's proceed this way: Please proceed with your question, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, for your help.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Groenewegen, you have this photograph in front of you, and you will receive a pointer from the usher. Can you mark on this photograph the place of the execution?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's pretty small, if we could mark it -- if we could bring it up a bit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The thing is I said we need to see the upper part, but on the other hand I don't want to establish or indicate one particular section.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can zoom in the upper part again more so at least we get the same --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I think it's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Groenewegen, if you can mark on this map now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it needs to be zoomed in further. Can you zoom in further? More or less make it the same size as the -- yeah. No, no, down, further down, further -- no, no, no. Yeah, yes. Yes. And you can even zoom in further. And another -- and further. Yeah. Now, is this better, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... to be zoomed in further? It can be zoomed in further.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's fine. This is fine. The important thing is for the witness to be able to help us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And your question is, do you think that with what you see in front of you, you can identify the place or the location of the execution or do you want us to zoom in further?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. This is fine. This is well possible. [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is the place you have marked as being the site of the execution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the dot might go a little more to the corner of the house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Could you put your initials against that dot, please? Or your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. If it is not in dispute that Mr. Franken in his testimony said something else, and marked the place differently, then there is no need to go into that with the Trial Chamber because then you will be able to see that we have two different photographs indicating two different locations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That becomes a question of submissions later on, or further questions by Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I'm not going to press the witness on this. I'm going to finish with this topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Groenewegen, thank you very much for your help, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This image will be saved and will be tendered in due course, I take it. Yes. Let's proceed. Do you have any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I am going to be finishing with one more topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Groenewegen, today you told us that you heard of these tragic incidents at the UN base on the night between the 12th and the 13th, the suicides, the deaths and everything that happened there. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you help us and tell us if you know where those persons were buried?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I can't tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please help us, tell us where this was happening, where are those bodies buried?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he's already answered the question, no? He told you he doesn't know. Correct me if I'm wrong but I think I heard him say no, he doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour, because the answer that I received was that he knew where this happened and where the bodies were buried.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I heard him distinctly say, "I can't tell you that." That's what I heard him say but if I am wrong, then the witness can correct me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sure that's the English. It's the B/C/S probably that may have been the problem because I'm sure everybody that was listening to the English heard him say he could not say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I see in line 15 on page 46 of the transcript, that it also says, "I can." I know. This is what confused me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But there is also that sign which indicates that that's incomplete.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Groenewegen, so your definite answer is that you do not know where the bodies are buried?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I do not know where the bodies were buried.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you arrived at the compound, did you hear that the bodies were buried somewhere inside the UN compound?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Absolutely no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Thank you, Mr. Groenewegen. We have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. Who is going next? Madam Fauveau is representing General Miletic and she will be putting some questions to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Mr. Groenewegen, when you gave your testimony before the Dutch authorities, you talked about a criminal network involved in the stealing of some of the UN equipment. Do you remember what this criminal network was?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: In the first place, I don't recall using the word "criminal network." However, I can confirm that theft of UN equipment or materials, that this happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show the witness Exhibit number 2D34, please? Can we turn to page 3, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Witness, in the first paragraph, you can read as follows: "[In English] [Previous translation continues] ... in Pale there was a criminal network which was involved in theft of UN goods and equipment. The local population indicated that the headquarters of the local Mafia was located in Pale. Some of the diesel cans stolen from OP Mike were later found in Pale." [Interpretation] Does this jog your memory?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Yes, it does do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can we agree that Pale was under Muslim control, the village of Pale?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And the diesel cans which were fuel cans and that had been stolen from the Mike OP had in fact been stolen by the Muslims; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Well, I did not myself see the thieves but if this was in Pale they must have been Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it true to factor that when you were in the Srebrenica enclave, you were never short of ammunition?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: We were never allowed to use munitions so I wouldn't dare speak of a shortage.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: At your debriefing, you said that you had been invited by some chief in Jaglici to have a coffee and share a coffee with him; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can you tell me whether this man was a military leader?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: That I cannot tell you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it true to factor that the refugees started arriving in Potocari on the 11th of July?
